title: Regular diagonal spectral pencil and diagonal gauge
notes: The pencil is \(D+U-EA\), with \(A=\operatorname{diag}(a_1,\ldots,a_n)\), distinct \(a_i\), and \(U_i^i=0\), which the notes say can always be achieved.
statement: On an interval, for a smooth complex matrix \(U\) and constant diagonal \(A\) with pairwise distinct entries, a diagonal invertible gauge \(g\) satisfying \(g_i^{\prime}=-U_{ii}g_i\) transforms \(g^{-1}(D+U-EA)g\) to a pencil with zero diagonal potential. A periodic gauge exists only when the diagonal holonomies permit it; the local assertion does not automatically preserve the periodic boundary condition.
reconstruction: The gauge equation and its global obstruction are explicit reconstructions; neither qualification is written.
fate: The regular-diagonal matrix setup appears in \citet[Ch.~III, \S2]{dubrovinmatveevnovikov1976nonlinear}; the paper was received 2 June 1975 and published in 1976. Receipt is not evidence of public circulation before this talk.
present_status: As of 10 November 2026, the result is established in the stated scope.

title: Formal diagonal resolvents and commuting matrix flows
notes: For diagonal constant \(B\), the notes seek \(\lambda_B=B+\sum_{j\ge1}\lambda_{j,B}E^{-j}\) satisfying \(\lambda_B^{\prime}=[\lambda_B,U-EA]\), and set \(U_t=[A,\lambda_{N+1,B}]\).
statement: Fix the formal diagonalization normalized to the identity at \(E=\infty\), and fix its diagonal integration constants. The equation determines the off-diagonal coefficients recursively because \(\operatorname{ad}A\) is invertible there. With the usual normalized diagonal resolvent, the resulting coefficients are differential polynomials in \(U\), and truncations give the matrix hierarchy. The displayed differential equation alone, without normalization, does not select a unique resolvent.
reconstruction: Normalization and the distinction between off-diagonal recursion and diagonal constants have been supplied; the notebook asserts polynomial dependence without giving that construction.
fate: Compare the normalized construction in \citet[Ch.~III, \S2]{dubrovinmatveevnovikov1976nonlinear} and its matrix elaboration in \citet[\S1]{dubrovin1977matrix}.
present_status: As of 10 November 2026, the result is established in the stated scope.

title: Isospectral Lax evolution
notes: All displayed flows are said to preserve the spectrum, since \(L_t=[L,M_N]\).
statement: For the spectral pencil, the auxiliary operator must give the compatible pair \([\partial_t-M_N,\partial_x+U-EA]=0\), with signs chosen consistently. For a periodic smooth potential and periodic auxiliary coefficients, the monodromy evolves by conjugation, so its characteristic polynomial and Floquet multipliers are constant. On a noncompact domain, preservation of an operator spectrum additionally requires a specified realization and suitable decay or boundedness conditions.
reconstruction: The notebook leaves the spectral meaning and domain unspecified; the periodic monodromy formulation makes one exact assertion that its calculation supports.
fate: This hierarchy is treated in \citet[Ch.~III, \S2]{dubrovinmatveevnovikov1976nonlinear}.
present_status: As of 10 November 2026, the result is established in the stated scope.

title: Stationary equations and the polynomial matrix Lax equation
notes: The stationary condition is \([L,M_N]=0\). The talk first writes \(\Lambda^{\prime}=[\Lambda,Q]\), but its lemma and proof reverse the commutator to \([Q,\Lambda]\), with \(Q=U-EA\).
statement: Restrict the commuting auxiliary differential operator to the local solution space of \((D+Q)\psi=0\); elimination of derivatives yields a polynomial matrix \(\Lambda(E,x)\). The condition \([D+Q,\Lambda]=0\) is exactly \(\Lambda^{\prime}=[\Lambda,Q]\). Hence \(\det(zI-\Lambda(E,x))\) is independent of \(x\).
reconstruction: \oursComputed\ The first sign in the notebook is retained and the two later signs are emended by direct expansion of the commutator.
fate: The stationary matrix reduction is part of \citet[Ch.~III, \S2]{dubrovinmatveevnovikov1976nonlinear}. The sign correction is checked algebraically from the notebook's own definition of \(Q\).
present_status: As of 10 November 2026, the result is established in the stated scope.

title: Algebraic finite-gap eigenfunction and spectral curve
notes: A polynomial pencil is called finite-gap when an eigenfunction is meromorphic on a fixed finite-genus covering of the \(E\)-plane, with essential singularities allowed over infinity. The proposed curve is \(R(z,E)=\det(zI-\Lambda(E))=0\).
statement: Take the normalization and compactification of the reduced irreducible spectral curve, with marked points above \(E=\infty\). On a regular component with generically simple eigenvalue, a common solution \((D+Q)\psi=0\), \(\Lambda\psi=z\psi\) defines the algebraic eigenline data; its normalized eigenfunction is meromorphic away from those points with prescribed exponential behavior there. This algebraic use of finite-gap is not itself a statement that a general matrix operator has a self-adjoint spectrum with finitely many real gaps.
reconstruction: Reduction, normalization, generic simplicity and the distinction from a real spectral-gap assertion are reconstructed hypotheses.
fate: For the matrix spectral-curve construction see \citet[Ch.~III, \S2]{dubrovinmatveevnovikov1976nonlinear}.
present_status: As of 10 November 2026, the result is established in the stated scope.

title: Bloch property of the common eigenfunction
notes: If \(U(x+T)=U(x)\), the simultaneous eigenfunction is said to be a Bloch function because translation commutes with \(\Lambda\).
statement: If both \(Q\) and the polynomial matrix \(\Lambda\) are \(T\)-periodic, their monodromy commutes with \(\Lambda(E,0)\). On each one-dimensional eigenspace at a simple point of the spectral curve, monodromy therefore acts by a scalar: \(\psi(x+T,P)=\mu(P)\psi(x,P)\). At a repeated eigenvalue one must choose a common eigenvector or allow generalized spectral data; an arbitrary vector in the repeated eigenspace need not be Bloch.
reconstruction: The simple-eigenline qualification and exceptional-point distinction make explicit the linear algebra behind the notebook remark.
fate: The Bloch/spectral-curve interpretation belongs to \citet[Ch.~III, \S2]{dubrovinmatveevnovikov1976nonlinear}.
present_status: As of 10 November 2026, the result is established in the stated scope.

title: Complete integrability of stationary matrix systems
notes: The stationary equations are called completely integrable Hamiltonian systems. Coefficients \(I_{ij}\) of \(R(z,E)\) are asserted to be commuting integrals.
statement: For the notebook's matrix equation \(\Lambda^{\prime}=[\Lambda,U-EA]\), direct differentiation proves only that the coefficients of \(\det(zI-\Lambda(E))\) are constants of motion. A claim of Liouville integrability additionally requires a specified Poisson manifold or symplectic leaf, commuting integrals and a rank count. The notebook supplies neither the Poisson bracket nor that phase space; consequently its full Hamiltonian assertion is only partially identifiable here. No complete modern integrability theorem for unspecified stationary data is substituted for it.
reconstruction: The exact consequence of the written Lax equation is separated from the stronger publication theorem. The latter has not been reproduced with all of its phase-space and independence hypotheses, so publication matching remains partial.
fate: The matrix integrability theorem is stated in \citet[Ch.~III, \S2, p.~117]{dubrovinmatveevnovikov1976nonlinear}; further details appear in \citet[\S\S1--3]{dubrovin1977matrix}.
present_status: As of 10 November 2026, matrix Hamiltonian integrability theorems are established in the cited works; the notebook's unqualified version is not a fully specified theorem.

title: Recovering matrix potentials with a fixed spectral curve
notes: The explicit problem asks for all finite-gap \(L\) with the same curve \(\Gamma\). The announced answer is a principal \(\pi\)-bundle over its Jacobian, where \(\pi\) is the diagonal invertible group modulo scalar matrices.
statement: Fix the regular diagonal leading matrix, the polynomial spectral invariants, marked points and local spectral normalization. For a smooth generic spectral curve, the nonsingular rank-one spectral data parametrize an open part of its Jacobian; eigenvector normalization retains a diagonal gauge torsor \(\pi\cong(\mathbb C^*)^{n-1}\). The reconstruction generally produces meromorphic potentials. The assertion must be restricted to the regular spectral-data locus and does not identify every singular or globally smooth real isospectral set with an entire compact Jacobian.
reconstruction: The open-locus and meromorphic qualifications, and the distinction between quotient and framed data, are explicit modern reconstructions. Dubrovin's published quotient notation is \(M_\Gamma/\pi=J(\Gamma)\); the open regular locus here describes the nonsingular-potential chart used in this reconstruction, not a verbatim restriction claimed for his entire algebraic parameter space.
fate: The answer is in \citet[Ch.~III, \S2, p.~117]{dubrovinmatveevnovikov1976nonlinear} and \citet[theorem on p.~269]{dubrovin1977matrix}. The latter was received 7 December 1976 and printed in volume 11 (1977); these dates must not be replaced by its later translation copyright.
present_status: As of 10 November 2026, the result is established in the stated scope.

title: Development of loops, curvature and torsion
notes: An ant moving on a cube and a curve developed from a plane are used to distinguish a displacement from a rotation, labelled torsion and curvature.
statement: For an affine connection with solder form \(\theta\) and connection form \(\omega\), torsion is \(T=d\theta+\omega\wedge\theta\), while curvature is \(\Omega=d\omega+\omega\wedge\omega\). Infinitesimal affine development relates their translational and rotational effects. An arbitrary finite loop's developed displacement is not by itself a torsion tensor; the intrinsic Levi-Civita geometry of a Euclidean polyhedral surface is torsion-free, with curvature concentrated in angle deficits at vertices.
reconstruction: The differential-form formulation and the warning about finite-loop development are explanatory reconstruction. The sketch does not specify a connection with nonzero torsion.
fate: This is an informal exposition of connection geometry. \citet[abstract and polyhedral construction]{regge1961relativity} gives the relevant pre-talk polyhedral curvature setting, but does not verify every assertion of the ant analogy.
present_status: As of 10 November 2026, the result is established in the stated scope.

title: Characteristic classes and basic geometry on polyhedra
notes: Gelfand asks how to build basic geometry, including characteristic classes, on higher-dimensional polyhedra.
statement: The notes specify no category of polyhedra, tangential structure, or desired definition. For a triangulated closed smooth \(n\)-manifold there is a precise existing instance: the mod-two sum of all \(p\)-simplices of its first barycentric subdivision represents the Poincare dual of \(w_{n-p}(TM)\). This example is evidence about the programme, not an identification of a new theorem being proposed.
reconstruction: The restricted manifold example is supplied to locate the discussion; no assertion is made for arbitrary singular polyhedra.
fate: The relevant pre-talk instance is \citet[Theorem 1 and its mod-two corollary, pp.~511--512]{halperintoledo1972stiefel}; the same construction is discussed explicitly in Fuchs's intervention on P000635.
present_status: As of 10 November 2026, the result is established in the stated scope.

title: General relativity on a lattice
notes: The notebook explicitly says: \ru{Задача: сделать общую относительность на решетках}.
statement: One can assign edge lengths to a simplicial complex, use flat metrics on its top-dimensional simplices, and concentrate curvature on codimension-two hinges. In four dimensions the Regge action is proportional to the sum of hinge areas times deficit angles. A mathematically definite new problem would have to specify a discretization, approximation class, limit, and convergence criterion; none is given here.
reconstruction: The simplicial realization is a historical comparison, not evidence that Gelfand specified that model or a convergence theorem.
fate: \citet[abstract]{regge1961relativity} had already proposed a polyhedral formulation of general relativity in 1961. The opened publisher record confirms that prior programme; this broad seminar request is not assigned a new open-problem identifier.
present_status: As of 10 November 2026, the historical request has established realizations; the notes do not specify a particular remaining convergence problem.

title: Reciprocal mathematics and physics curricula
notes: The physics list names Feynman--Hibbs, Feynman's lectures and statistical mechanics, Landau--Lifshitz, Berestetskii--Lifshitz--Pitaevskii, and Dirac. The mathematics list includes representations, pseudodifferential and Fourier integral operators, Riemann--Roch, singularities and topological cycles.
statement: This is a pedagogical proposal to teach established mathematical and physical subjects across the two communities. It states no common theorem, prerequisite graph, or new research question. The separate functional equation for a polynomial is indexed in the next item.
reconstruction: No individual textbook edition is reconstructed from abbreviated names, and bare topic names are not inflated into conjectures.
fate: The notebook is the direct evidence for the curriculum. Its sole displayed mathematical theorem is independently matched below to \citet{bernstein1972continuation}.
present_status: As of 10 November 2026, this remains a historical teaching programme, with no theorem-level status to resolve.

title: The polynomial functional equation
notes: The example under singularities is \(L P^\lambda=a(\lambda)P^{\lambda-1}\).
statement: For a nonzero polynomial \(P\in\mathbb C[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\), there are a nonzero polynomial \(b(s)\in\mathbb C[s]\) and a differential operator \(Q(s)\) with coefficients in \(\mathbb C[x,s]\) satisfying \(Q(s)P^{s+1}=b(s)P^s\) in the formal localization module. Taking \(s=\lambda-1\) gives the notebook's convention. Allowing polynomial dependence of the operator on the exponent is essential.
reconstruction: The coefficient ring, formal meaning of the powers and shift of the exponent are supplied.
fate: \citet[Theorem 1\(^{\prime}\), p.~26 of the Russian original]{bernstein1972continuation} supplies the polynomial-parameter differential functional equation; the paper appeared in 1972, before the seminar.
present_status: As of 10 November 2026, the result is established in the stated scope.

title: Quark content, spin and resonance shorthand
notes: The notes introduce three spin-\(1/2\) quarks \(u,d,s\), label baryons spin \(1/2\) and mesons spin zero, and describe resonances as orbital excitations.
statement: In the simplest constituent model, conventional baryons have valence content \(qqq\), while conventional mesons have \(q\bar q\). Their spins are obtained by coupling constituent spins and orbital angular momentum; baryons need not have spin \(1/2\), and mesons need not have spin zero. An orbital-excitation model describes some resonances but is not a definition of every hadronic resonance.
reconstruction: The spin labels are restricted to examples; their literal universal reading is false even for the spin-\(3/2\) baryon discussed later on the same page.
fate: The pre-talk review \citet[\S I and Appendix I]{levinfrankfurt1968quark} already includes spin-\(3/2\) baryons and spin-one mesons. These are old model distinctions, not a later correction discovered by this seminar.
present_status: As of 10 November 2026, the result is established in the stated scope.

title: Flavor tensor products for mesons and baryons
notes: The page lists \(\bar3\otimes3=1\oplus8\), \(3^{\otimes3}=1\oplus8\oplus8\oplus10\), and \(3\otimes3=\bar3\oplus6\).
statement: For the complex defining representation \(V\) of \(SU(3)\), \(V^*\otimes V=\mathbb C\oplus\mathfrak{sl}_3\), \(\Lambda^2V\cong V^*\), and \(V^{\otimes3}\cong\mathbb C\oplus\mathfrak{sl}_3^{\oplus2}\oplus\operatorname{Sym}^3V\). The displayed dimensions are \(9=1+8\), \(9=3+6\), and \(27=1+8+8+10\). These are exact representation identities; assigning them to flavor multiplets is a physical model.
reconstruction: The vector-space notation distinguishes an exact tensor decomposition from empirical approximate flavor symmetry.
fate: The quark-model context predates the talk: \citet[pp.~214--215; publisher metadata]{gellmann1964schematic}. The identities themselves follow directly from tensor symmetry and are explicitly present in the notebook.
present_status: As of 10 November 2026, the result is established in the stated scope.

title: The additive-quark total-cross-section ratio
notes: For high-energy baryon--baryon and baryon--meson scattering, the ratio is recorded as \(3/2\), to about ten percent; particle and antiparticle cross sections are said to coincide.
statement: If a high-energy additive constituent model assigns the same effective scattering strength to each valence quark or antiquark, with negligible multiple-scattering and wavefunction corrections, constituent counting gives \(\sigma(BB)/\sigma(BM)\approx9/6=3/2\). Equality of particle and antiparticle total cross sections concerns an asymptotic scattering statement under additional analyticity and growth assumptions, not an exact equality at all energies. The stated ten-percent agreement is a historical estimate without a specified dataset.
reconstruction: The factorization assumptions and separation from an asymptotic theorem are supplied; no present experimental error bound is inferred.
fate: \citet[Introduction, p.~108, and \S VII]{levinfrankfurt1968quark} explicitly discusses this ratio under a Pomeranchuk-limit assumption before 1975.
present_status: As of 10 November 2026, the result is established in the stated scope.

title: The historical absence of pentaquarks
notes: The notes say that a \(qqqq\bar q\) configuration has not been observed.
statement: As a dated empirical remark this concerns the evidence available to the speaker in November 1975. It is not a representation-theoretic prohibition: \(3^{\otimes4}\otimes\bar3\) contains color singlets. A later observation of resonances consistent with such minimal valence content does not by itself determine a compact five-quark rather than molecular internal structure.
reconstruction: The minimal-content and internal-structure distinction is supplied to prevent the historical sentence being read as a theorem.
fate: \citet[abstract]{lhcb2015pentaquark}, first submitted 13 July 2015, reported hidden-charm structures consistent with pentaquark states. This changes the historical observational context; it does not settle their microscopic binding mechanism.
present_status: As of 10 November 2026, the 1975 non-observation statement is historical and cannot be repeated as a present exclusion.

title: Color, fermion statistics and singlet tensors
notes: The symmetric \(uuu\) state of \(\Delta^{++}\) motivates three colors and an antisymmetric color factor; the notes also display a colorless meson sum.
statement: For three identical spin-\(1/2\) quarks in a symmetric spatial, spin and flavor state, the antisymmetric tensor \(\varepsilon_{abc}\) in color \(\mathbb C^3\) supplies the required fermionic antisymmetry. A color-singlet meson contraction is \(\sum_a\bar q_a q_a\), while a baryon contraction is \(\varepsilon_{abc}q_aq_bq_c\). The middle term of the notebook's meson sum has two barred factors and must be emended.
reconstruction: The fully antisymmetric color tensor is the modern formulation of the notebook's proposal. Historical paraquark and three-triplet models are precursors, not literally identical to modern QCD.
fate: Pre-talk precedents are \citet[publisher record]{greenberg1964paraquark} and \citet[abstract]{hannambu1965triplet}; both dates and the latter's double-\(SU(3)\) model were checked.
present_status: As of 10 November 2026, the result is established in the stated scope.

title: Approximate flavor symmetry and exact color gauge invariance
notes: The discussion contrasts approximately valid flavor \(SU(3)\) with exact color \(SU(3)\), suggests four flavors, and contains the isolated phrase that the Lagrangian cannot be invariant under flavor times color.
statement: For quark fields in the fundamental color representation, a common flavor-independent kinetic term is invariant under global flavor rotations and local color gauge transformations. A nondegenerate quark-mass matrix breaks the global flavor symmetry while preserving color gauge invariance. Four flavors give an approximate global \(SU(4)\) only in a mass-degenerate idealization; adding a flavor does not change the color group. The isolated blanket denial of invariance cannot be reconciled literally with the next page without this distinction.
reconstruction: The mass-matrix qualification is reconstructed. The numerical 20--30 percent accuracy and dating of a fourth flavor are not converted into rigorous statements.
fate: Four-quark weak-current models already appear in \citet[abstract]{glashowiliopoulosmaiani1970weak}, published 1 October 1970. This verifies a pre-talk four-flavor precedent, not the notebook's approximate chronology or percentage.
present_status: As of 10 November 2026, the result is established in the stated scope.

title: Noncommutative electrical engineering
notes: Gelfand proposes a classical version described as noncommutative electrical engineering, with a diagram.
statement: No circuit equations, class of networks, noncommutative coefficient algebra, boundary conditions or assertion to test are specified. The strongest recoverable content is a programme to interpret classical non-Abelian gauge fields in an electrical-network language.

title: Variational symmetries and conserved currents
notes: The line before the confinement proposal relates conserved currents to the presence of symmetry by a two-way arrow.
statement: For a finite-order local Lagrangian with sufficiently differentiable fields and coefficients, an infinitesimal variational symmetry depending on constant parameters gives a current whose divergence is a linear combination of the Euler--Lagrange expressions and hence vanishes on solutions. Boundary terms and currents differing by identically conserved improvements must be treated consistently. A symmetry depending on arbitrary functions instead yields differential identities among the Euler--Lagrange expressions. Gauge charges further depend on boundary conditions; the bare arrow is not a universal bijection between every current and every gauge redundancy.
reconstruction: The finite-parameter and arbitrary-function cases are separated, with the local variational and boundary hypotheses supplied. This mathematical assertion is distinct from the unformalized electrical-engineering programme in 1975-377.8.
fate: \citet[\S1, Theorems I--II]{noether1918invariant} states the two classical results. The opened text is Tavel's 1971 English translation of the 1918 paper; its later arXiv deposit is not its first publication.
present_status: As of 10 November 2026, the result is established in the stated scope.

title: A linearly rising potential in four-dimensional pure gauge theory
notes: The proposed outcome is \(E(R)\sim R\) for non-Abelian fields, contrasted with \(R^{-1}\) in the Abelian case. Colorless composites should have finite mass while an isolated color charge is excluded from the finite-energy spectrum.
statement: A definite reconstruction is the zero-temperature infinite-volume four-dimensional pure \(SU(N)\) Yang--Mills theory, \(N\ge2\), with external fundamental charges and a renormalized rectangular Wilson loop: after removal of perimeter/self-energy terms, \(V(R)=-\lim_{T\to\infty}T^{-1}\log\langle W(R,T)\rangle\) should obey \(\lim_{R\to\infty}V(R)/R=\sigma>0\). Dynamical fundamental matter must be excluded for an asymptotic unbroken string. Noncommutativity alone, without dimension, matter content, phase and continuum hypotheses, is insufficient.
reconstruction: The formal action explicitly contains \(d^4x\), indicating the dimension four. The notebook does not specify the continuum/regularization or matter-content conditions. The reconstructed four-dimensional pure-gauge assertion is the unresolved part; a bare infinite mass term is not the meaning of confinement.
fate: \citet[\S IV]{wilson1974confinement} gives the pre-talk strong-coupling lattice mechanism. \citet[\S5]{jaffewitten2000yangmills} separates confinement from the existence-and-mass-gap problem; the official current description \citep{clay2026yangmills} still lists the latter as unresolved. Lattice strong coupling does not establish a continuum area law.
present_status: As of 10 November 2026, the reconstructed four-dimensional continuum area-law statement remains unproved; fixed-lattice and lower-dimensional results do not close it.
worth: Worth retaining as a precise research problem, but a bounded chapter cannot supply the missing four-dimensional continuum construction and positive string tension; dimensional and screening qualifications are the useful contribution here.

title: Infinitely heavy charges and suppression of pair creation
notes: Taking quark mass \(M\to\infty\) is used to discard quark-pair diagrams and retain paths of two external charges.
statement: Static source worldlines arise from an infinite external-mass limit after subtracting their rest energies. Removing dynamical quark loops is a separate pure-gauge or quenched assumption, or a decoupling limit for every dynamical quark mass. Infinite mass of the two probes alone does not prevent light dynamical quarks from screening them and breaking the string.
reconstruction: The separation of probe and sea-quark masses is a necessary reconstruction that the diagrams do not make explicit.
fate: The loop and screening discussion is already present in \citet[\S II, especially the nearby-vacuum-loop discussion]{wilson1974confinement}.
present_status: As of 10 November 2026, the result is established in the stated scope.

title: Wilson loops and extraction of a static energy
notes: The field integral contains \(\operatorname{tr}\exp(i\oint A)\); its meaning is given by an ordered product. The rectangle has sides \(R,T\). One line says \(W\to ET\), whereas the next page uses \(e^{-iET}\).
statement: The gauge-invariant loop is the trace of the path-ordered holonomy. In a Euclidean regulated formulation with a positive transfer operator, a rectangular loop has a spectral expansion \(\sum_n c_n(R)e^{-E_n(R)T}\), and nonzero overlap with the lowest state yields \(-T^{-1}\log\langle W(R,T)\rangle\to V(R)\), after source-energy subtraction. In real time the amplitude is \(e^{-iET}\), so writing it as \(e^{iW}\) gives \(W=-ET\).
reconstruction: \oursComputed\ The phase sign is checked against \(e^{-iET}\). The Euclidean spectral interpretation, overlap hypothesis and subtraction are supplied. Path ordering is already present in the notebook's product definition and is not an omitted operation.
fate: This construction and its physical interpretation precede the talk in \citet[\S\S II--III]{wilson1974confinement}.
present_status: As of 10 November 2026, the result is established in the stated scope.

title: Worldline phases and the area-law criterion
notes: The path-sum explanation uses the phase \(e^{-iET}\), treats an antiparticle as a reversed worldline, and proceeds to \(W(C)\sim\operatorname{area}(C)=RT\), hence \(E(R)\sim R\).
statement: For a large rectangular Euclidean loop, an asymptotic law \(\log\langle W(R,T)\rangle=-\sigma RT+\text{perimeter and subleading terms}\) implies the linear static energy after the appropriate successive limits and perimeter subtraction. A worldline representation identifies the observable but does not prove its area law. The latter is an independent dynamical assertion, not a consequence of reversing one trajectory.
reconstruction: The conditional implication and order of limits separate the valid extraction method from the unproved dynamical step.
fate: The loop/area-law criterion was formulated in \citet[\S II]{wilson1974confinement}; its unresolved continuum use is item 1975-377.10.
present_status: As of 10 November 2026, the conditional criterion is established; proving its premise in four-dimensional continuum pure Yang--Mills theory remains the problem indexed above.

title: Gaussian Abelian loop and the Coulomb potential
notes: The Abelian field integral becomes the exponential of a double line integral of a propagator; the rectangular-loop expression is a term proportional to \(T\) plus a term proportional to \(e^2T/R\).
statement: For a centered Gaussian Euclidean gauge field with covariance \(D_{\mu\nu}\) and a conserved regularized loop current \(J\), \(\langle e^{ie(A,J)}\rangle=\exp[-e^2(J,DJ)/2]\). In four-dimensional Maxwell theory, removing the divergent self-energies of two opposite static charges yields \(V(R)=-e^2/(4\pi R)\) in rationalized units. Coincident-point integrals require a regulator; the sign and factor in the notebook depend on propagator and real/Euclidean-time conventions.
reconstruction: The regulator, charge signs, units and explicit covariance identity are reconstructed. The \(R^{-1}\) law assumes three spatial dimensions and a massless noncompact Maxwell field.
fate: The Abelian comparison is part of the pre-talk analysis in \citet[\S II]{wilson1974confinement}.
present_status: As of 10 November 2026, the result is established in the stated scope.

title: Why the non-Abelian integral is not Gaussian
notes: The final comparison points to the commutator term in \(F\), and also to multiple extrema for compact Abelian variables.
statement: In a non-Abelian gauge theory, \(F=dA+A\wedge A\), so the action contains cubic and quartic interactions in a local gauge potential and is not a Gaussian functional. Compact lattice \(U(1)\) has a nonlinear periodic plaquette action even though its group is Abelian. Thus Gaussian Maxwell calculations cannot decide the infrared phase of either interacting non-Abelian theory or arbitrary compact Abelian models.
reconstruction: The distinction between a linear Abelian continuum field and a compact lattice model makes the scope of the comparison explicit.
fate: Both compact Abelian and non-Abelian lattice formulations occur in \citet[\S\S III--IV]{wilson1974confinement}; their strong-coupling behavior is not exclusive to non-Abelian groups.
present_status: As of 10 November 2026, the result is established in the stated scope.

title: Zero-curvature compatibility for two auxiliary equations
notes: The equation is \([L_1-\partial_y,L_2-\partial_t]=0\), with scalar differential operators in \(x\), monic leading terms, and constant next coefficients. Gelfand emphasizes the symmetry of the auxiliary variables.
statement: For sufficiently differentiable operator coefficients, compatibility of \(\psi_y=L_1\psi\), \(\psi_t=L_2\psi\) is \(\partial_yL_2-\partial_tL_1=[L_1,L_2]\). The same operator identity makes sense for matrices or operators in other variables, but existence of a common solution requires suitable analytic or formal initial-value conditions. The displayed equation alone is the zero-curvature identity; it does not by itself construct a nonlinear solution.
reconstruction: The equivalent sign convention is obtained by expanding the commutator. The original scalar differential setting is distinguished from Gelfand's broader operator analogy.
fate: \citet[Theorem 1 and Corollary 1, pp.~291--292]{krichever1976zakharov} constructs solutions in this form. The manuscript was received 8 October 1975 and presented to the Academy on 24 October; neither date alone proves public availability before the February talk.
present_status: As of 10 November 2026, the result is established in the stated scope.

title: Formal wave-function recursion and its normalization
notes: The ansatz is \(\psi=e^{kx+k^ny}\sum_{j\ge0}\xi_jk^{-j}\), \(\xi_0=1\). The written normalization is \(\xi_j(0,y,t)=0\) for \(j>1\).
statement: For \(L=D^n+\sum_{i=0}^{n-2}u_iD^i\), formal coefficient comparison in \((L-\partial_y)\psi=0\) recursively determines \(\partial_x\xi_j\). Prescribing \(\xi_j(0,y,t)\) for every \(j\ge1\) fixes the integration functions. A nonzero constant \(D^{n-1}\) coefficient requires the corresponding \(k^{n-1}y\) term in the exponential phase; it is incompatible with the unmodified displayed phase.
reconstruction: The normalization bound is emended to \(j\ge1\), and either the next coefficient must vanish or the phase must change. This is a formal calculation and asserts no convergence.
fate: The more general polynomial phase in \citet[conditions 1--2 preceding Theorem 1]{krichever1976zakharov} makes the missing phase term explicit.
present_status: As of 10 November 2026, the result is established in the stated scope.

title: Recovering an operator from a normalized formal wave
notes: Conversely, every normalized series is said to determine an operator up to a residual of order \(k^{-1}\); the final proof applies uniqueness to that residual.
statement: For a normalized formal wave \(e^{kx+k^ny}(1+\sum_{j\ge1}\xi_jk^{-j})\), comparison of nonnegative powers of \(k\) uniquely gives a monic \(L_n\), with no \(D^{n-1}\) term, for which \(e^{-kx-k^ny}(L_n-\partial_y)\psi=O(k^{-1})\). If the wave also satisfies the nonspecial Baker--Akhiezer conditions below, the residual has the same allowed finite poles and zero leading normalization; uniqueness makes it identically zero. For an arbitrary formal wave only the residual statement follows.
reconstruction: The two distinct stages, formal cancellation and global uniqueness, are separated to avoid silently assuming the analytic conclusion.
fate: This is the proof mechanism of \citet[Theorem 1, pp.~291--292]{krichever1976zakharov}.
present_status: As of 10 November 2026, the result is established in the stated scope.

title: Commuting scalar operators of orders two and three
notes: Gelfand's school problem asks when \(L_1=-D^2+u\) and \(L_2=D^3+v_1D+v_2\) commute, with an answer in elliptic functions or elliptic curves.
statement: On an interval with smooth complex coefficients, direct comparison of powers of \(D\) gives \(v_1=-3u/2+c_1\), \(v_2=-3u^{\prime}/4+c_2\), and \(u^{(3)}-6uu^{\prime}+4c_1u^{\prime}=0\). Integrating twice gives \((u^{\prime})^2=2u^3-4c_1u^2+2c_3u+c_4\). The solutions are elliptic functions on a nonsingular cubic, or their rational/trigonometric/hyperbolic degenerations, restricted away from poles.
reconstruction: \oursComputed\ The coefficient comparison and integration constants were independently checked. This reconstructs a classical exercise, including degenerate cubics, and makes no priority claim.
fate: \citet[\S3, equations (2)--(3)]{mulase1990geometric} gives this classical calculation in an equivalent normalization and traces the order-two/order-three case to Wallenberg (1903). The historical attribution is secondary within that research article; the displayed calculation was read and independently expanded here.
present_status: As of 10 November 2026, the result is established in the stated scope.
speaker: I. M. Gelfand (intervention)

title: Algebraic operator versus merely formal asymptotics
notes: An operator is called algebraic when its formal wave extends meromorphically to a compact curve away from one marked point, with poles independent of \(x,y,t\). Gelfand stresses that an asymptotic expansion usually diverges.
statement: The intended data are a smooth projective curve \(X\), a marked point \(P\), a local coordinate \(z=k^{-1}\), and a fixed pole divisor away from \(P\). The normalized wave must actually define a holomorphic function near the puncture after removal of its exponential singularity, and a meromorphic function elsewhere. A formal Laurent series does not determine such a global meromorphic function without convergence and continuation conditions.
reconstruction: Convergence of the exponential-normalized series and fixed divisor are imposed as parts of this definition, not derived from the coefficient recursion.
fate: The analytic data appear explicitly before \citet[Theorem 1]{krichever1976zakharov}.
present_status: As of 10 November 2026, the result is established in the stated scope.

The strongest recoverable content is a request to understand when the formal wave data determine an analytic or algebraic object; there is no unique theorem or quantified conjecture to reconstruct.

title: Existence and uniqueness of the Baker-Akhiezer wave
notes: The theorem attributed in the notes to Akhiezer allows a fixed set of poles and says that \(\psi e^{-kx-k^ny}=1+o(k^{-1})\), with uniqueness up to proportionality.
statement: Let \(X\) be a smooth compact complex curve of genus \(g\), \(P\in X\), and \(D\) an effective nonspecial divisor of degree \(g\) disjoint from \(P\). Fix a local coordinate \(k^{-1}\) and polynomial exponential phase. For times in the open set on which the normalized interpolation problem is nonsingular, there is a unique wave meromorphic on \(X\setminus\{P\}\), with poles bounded by \(D\), whose exponential-normalized germ is \(1+O(k^{-1})\). With leading coefficient fixed to one, there is no remaining scalar ambiguity.
reconstruction: Nonspeciality, degree, open time domain and the large-O correction are supplied. The source's Akhiezer attribution is retained historically; its stated multiparameter version is matched to Krichever's publication.
fate: \citet[conditions 1--2 and Theorem 1]{krichever1976zakharov} gives the matching construction with a general-position divisor and a \(1+\sum\xi_jk^{-j}\) expansion.
present_status: As of 10 November 2026, the result is established in the stated scope.

title: The elliptic example requires a meromorphic correction factor
notes: The elliptic illustration writes an exponential involving the Weierstrass zeta function.
statement: The Weierstrass zeta function is quasi-periodic, so \(e^{x\zeta(z)}\) alone is generally not a single-valued function on the elliptic curve. A Baker--Akhiezer function needs a sigma- or theta-function ratio whose quasi-period multiplier cancels that of the exponential, together with the prescribed fixed pole and normalization. This is the genus-one instance of the preceding construction.
reconstruction: The displayed exponential is treated as the essential-singularity factor, not a complete global formula.
fate: The finite-pole and global-meromorphic requirements in \citet[conditions 1--2]{krichever1976zakharov} identify exactly what the isolated exponential omits.
present_status: As of 10 November 2026, the result is established in the stated scope.

title: Differential operator ring over a differential algebra
notes: \(B\) is a commutative unital complex algebra with derivation \(b\mapsto b^{\prime}\); the ring \(B[D]\) has \(Db-bD=b^{\prime}\).
statement: For any commutative unital \(\mathbb C\)-algebra \(B\) and derivation \(\delta\), the Ore extension \(B[D;\delta]\) consists of finite sums \(\sum b_iD^i\), with multiplication determined by \(Db=bD+\delta(b)\). This definition remains meaningful when \(B\) is not a field; existence of a division ring of fractions requires extra hypotheses.
reconstruction: The Ore-extension notation and the limitation about fractions are supplied; no analytic ellipticity is implicit in the ring definition.
fate: The algebra is used explicitly in \citet[\S2]{drinfeld1977commutative}. The defining construction is background, distinct from the new geometric interpretation.
present_status: As of 10 November 2026, the result is established in the stated scope.

title: The claim that all commutative subrings come from smooth curves
notes: With \(A=H^0(X\setminus\{P\},\mathcal O_X)\), the notes say that no other commutative subrings occur and attribute this to Shabat.
statement: The smooth-curve formulation is too broad without restrictions. For example, the commutative subring \(\mathbb C[D^2,D^3]\subset\mathbb C[D]\) has a cuspidal spectrum; it is not the function ring of a smooth affine curve. Geometric classifications must allow singular spectral curves and suitable torsion-free sheaves, or restrict to subrings with a specified smooth spectral curve and regularity properties.
reconstruction: The cusp example is a direct counterexample to the unrestricted literal reading; it does not disprove a more qualified theorem that the speaker may have intended. \ours\ The cusp obstruction is elementary: \(t\) is integral over \(\mathbb C[t^2,t^3]\), since it satisfies \(T^2-t^2=0\), but it does not lie in that ring. Thus the ring is not normal, whereas the coordinate ring of a smooth affine curve is normal.
fate: \citet[\S2]{drinfeld1977commutative} treats a fixed smooth pointed curve, while \citet[\S2, Main Theorem]{mulase1990geometric} explicitly allows singular curves. Searches did not identify an exact Shabat theorem with the notebook's stated quantifiers.
present_status: As of 10 November 2026, the literal claim is false and the intended attribution remains unresolved; this is not evidence of an open classification problem.

title: Elliptic homomorphisms and their rank
notes: Every nonzero image \(\varphi(a)\) is required to have an invertible leading coefficient. The notes derive \(\operatorname{ord}\varphi(a)=n\deg_P(a)\) and call \(n\) the rank.
statement: Let \(X\) be a smooth connected projective complex curve, \(P\in X\), and \(A=H^0(X\setminus\{P\},\mathcal O_X)\). A unital \(\mathbb C\)-homomorphism \(\varphi:A\to B[D]\) is a Krichever homomorphism if every nonzero image has unit leading coefficient and some image has positive order. Then \(\operatorname{ord}\varphi(a)=n(-v_P(a))\) for nonconstant \(a\), with an integer \(n>0\). Because the pole-order semigroup is cofinite, \(n\) equals the greatest common divisor of the positive operator orders.
reconstruction: The nontrivial positive-order condition, smooth connected curve and meaning of degree are made explicit. Elliptic here is algebraic terminology, not a real principal-symbol positivity condition.
fate: The definition and rank lemma occur in \citet[\S2, preceding Proposition 2]{drinfeld1977commutative}, received 14 April 1976 and published in 1977.
present_status: As of 10 November 2026, the result is established in the stated scope.

title: A homomorphism encoded by a filtered module
notes: Take \(M=B[D]\), let \(B\) act on the left and \(A\) on the right through \(\varphi\), filter by operator order, and let \(\nabla\) be left multiplication by \(D\).
statement:
The filtration has \(M_{-1}=0\), \(M= igcup_{i\ge0}M_i\), and each \(M_i/M_{i-1}\) is free of rank one over \(B\). The operator \(
abla\) commutes with \(A\), satisfies \(
abla(bm)=b
abla m+b^{\prime}m\), and induces isomorphisms on successive graded pieces. A nonzero \(a\in A\) shifts filtration by \(n\deg_P(a)\) and gives a graded isomorphism. Conversely, these axioms and a generator of \(M_0\) identify \(M\) with \(B[D]\) and recover the right multiplication homomorphism, up to invertible scalar gauge.
reconstruction: Exhaustiveness, the initial zero piece and local freeness are stated explicitly; the converse follows by induction on filtration degree.
fate: \citet[Proposition 2 and its proof]{drinfeld1977commutative} gives the precise module correspondence.
present_status: As of 10 November 2026, the result is established in the stated scope.

title: From order filtrations to sheaves and a pole at infinity
notes: The filtered \(A\otimes B\)-module is reinterpreted as a sheaf on \(X\) with a filtration, and \(\nabla\) as a connection singular at infinity.
statement: A compatible exhaustive good filtration on a finite-type \(A\otimes B\)-module allows extension across \(P\) by lattices determined by pole order. For rank one and a nonsingular spectral curve, the regular geometric case gives a line bundle and an \(\mathcal O_X\)-linear relative operator \(\nabla:L\to L(P)\) obeying the \(B\)-Leibniz rule. Arbitrary filtered modules without the freeness, growth and multiplication-isomorphism conditions need not define this geometric object.
reconstruction: The word connection means differentiation in the coefficient parameter, not a flat holomorphic connection on all tangent directions of the curve.
fate: The exact extension machinery is \citet[Proposition 1, Corollary 1, and Proposition 2]{drinfeld1977commutative}; the March talks unpack its rank-one case.
present_status: As of 10 November 2026, the result is established in the stated scope.

title: Recovering a radial profile from its joint frequency array
notes: For an elastic sphere, recover the medium parameter from all \(\lambda_{k\ell}\). The written equation contains both a \(\lambda^2 f^2\) term and a separate eigenvalue on the right, with an inconsistent sign.
statement: The identified scalar radial model is \(y^{\prime\prime}+[\lambda_{k\ell}^2f(r)^2-\ell(\ell+1)/r^2]y=0\), \(0<r<1\). Require the regular solution at zero and a fixed real homogeneous separated condition \(\alpha y(1)+\beta y^{\prime}(1)=0\), \((\alpha,\beta)\ne(0,0)\). For the monotone reconstruction assume \(f>0\), \(f(1)=1\), and \(q(r)=rf(r)\) strictly increasing from zero to one; smoothness and \(q^{\prime}>0\) suffice for the formulas below. The data retain both radial and angular indices. This scalar equation does not recover every Lam'e parameter of an arbitrary elastic solid.
reconstruction: The corrected equation and endpoint conditions come from the identified publication. Positivity and strict smooth monotonicity delimit a regular version; the notebook writes only monotonicity and omits boundary conditions.
fate: \citet[equations (1)--(2) and Theorem 2]{brodskii1976spectral} is the exact publication match for the reported scalar problem, published in volume 31(4), 1976. The earliest public version is not established: a related 1975 torsional-oscillation paper is recorded as an unresolved primary-source lead in the audit. The B label records authorship relative to the reporter, with this chronology qualification.
present_status: As of 10 November 2026, the result is established in the stated scope.

title: Semiclassical spectral sampling of the radial action
notes: With \(q=rf\) monotone, the notes use a turning point \(H(\tau)\), an action integral, and pairs \(\tau_{k\ell}=\sqrt{\ell(\ell+1)}/\lambda_{k\ell}\), \(m_{k\ell}=(k+1/4+C)/\sqrt{\ell(\ell+1)}\).
statement: For \(\ell\ge1\), write \(L_\ell=\sqrt{\ell(\ell+1)}\), \(H=q^{-1}\), and \[m(\tau)=\pi^{-1}\int_{H(\tau)}^1\sqrt{\tau^{-2}f(r)^2-r^{-2}}\,dr,\qquad 0<\tau<1.\] In the smooth one-turning-point regime, the leading quantization relation samples this action as \(m(\tau_{k\ell})=(k+\delta_{k\ell})/L_\ell+o(1)\) along joint high-frequency limits in compact interior \(\tau\)-ranges. The bounded phase \(\delta_{k\ell}\) depends on the endpoint condition; it is not a universal constant. Dense limiting ratios recover the continuous action curve.
reconstruction: The factor \(1/\pi\), bounded boundary phase, limiting interpretation and interior restriction are supplied. Individual finite-index pairs are not asserted to lie exactly on a smooth dispersion graph.
fate: \citet[Theorem 1 and equation (4)]{brodskii1976spectral} supplies the asymptotic sampling, with the boundary correction retained explicitly. Exact overlap with the bibliographically attested 1975 precursor remains unverified; no priority date is inferred from the 1975 receipt stamp.
present_status: As of 10 November 2026, the result is established in the stated scope.

title: The Abel inversion and its missing normalization
notes: The inverse \(\psi=q^{-1}\) is written as an exponential with coefficient 2 and kernel \((\tau^2-\eta^2)^{-1/2}\); the lower endpoint is absent. The preceding action integral lacks \(1/\pi\).
statement: For positive smooth \(f\) with \(q(0)=0\), \(q(1)=1\), \(q^{\prime}>0\), let \(M(\tau)=\tau m(\tau)\) with the normalized action of the previous item. Then for \(0<\eta<1\), \[\log\psi(\eta)=2\int_\eta^1\frac{M^{\prime}(\tau)}{\sqrt{\tau^2-\eta^2}}\,d\tau.\] If the notebook's unnormalized action is retained, the multiplier must instead be \(2/\pi\). Knowing \(\psi\) recovers \(q\) by inversion and \(f(r)=q(r)/r\).
reconstruction: \oursComputed\ The lower endpoint and normalization are emendations checked by composing the two Abel kernels and with the constant profile. The complete short derivation and a reproducible numerical check are supplied in the research log and check script.
fate: \citet[Theorem 2, equations (5)--(6)]{brodskii1976spectral} gives this application. The Abel inversion mechanism is classical; \citet[Theorems 2.2.1 and 2.2.3, historical Remark 2.2.2]{paternainsalouhlmann2022geometric} distinguishes the older Herglotz travel-time inversion from Brodskii's spectral sampling.
present_status: As of 10 November 2026, the result is established in the stated scope.

title: Compatibility of an overdetermined spectral array
notes: The source calls the inverse problem overdetermined and asks when it is solvable; it mentions density and a one-to-one relation between spectral parameters.
statement: For the fixed radial boundary problem above, a necessary condition is that its joint high-frequency samples approach a continuous monotone action/dispersion graph compatible with a positive increasing inverse profile. Such leading asymptotic compatibility is not sufficient for an arbitrary entire array to equal the exact spectrum of that profile: finitely many modified eigenvalues leave the limiting graph unchanged but may violate exact spectral constraints.
reconstruction: The last observation separates a range theorem for a leading action transform from a range theorem for all exact frequencies. The notebook does not specify a complete topology, boundary model or list of sufficient conditions.
fate: \citet[corollary after Theorem 2]{brodskii1976spectral} states a necessary condition, not a full necessary-and-sufficient spectral-range theorem. No claim that the whole range question was solved is made here.
present_status: As of 10 November 2026, the identified publication establishes the stated necessary compatibility and inversion results. The notes are insufficient to isolate an additional exact residual range problem, so no C classification is manufactured from the omitted endpoint data.

title: Barycentric cycles representing Stiefel-Whitney classes
notes: Fuchs observes that the sum of all edges of an arbitrary triangulation need not be a mod-two cycle, whereas it is a cycle after first barycentric subdivision; the dual classes are Stiefel--Whitney classes.
statement: Let \(K\) be a smooth finite triangulation of a closed smooth \(n\)-manifold \(M\), and let \(K^{\prime}\) be its first barycentric subdivision. For each \(0\le p\le n\), the sum \(c_p\) of all \(p\)-simplices of \(K^{\prime}\), with coefficients in \(\mathbb F_2\), is a cycle and \([c_p]=w_{n-p}(TM)\cap[M]\). In particular, the all-edge cycle represents the homology class dual to \(w_{n-1}\), not generally to \(w_1\). For manifolds with boundary a relative formulation is needed.
reconstruction: The dimension indexing and closed-manifold hypotheses are reconstructed. The notebook drawings support the parity motivation but do not replace the characteristic-class theorem.
fate: The precise mod-two statement was published in \citet[Theorem 1 and its corollary, pp.~511--512]{halperintoledo1972stiefel}; their remarks also discuss the PL extension.
present_status: As of 10 November 2026, the result is established in the stated scope.
speaker: D. B. Fuchs (intervention)

title: Parity of the simplex count and Euler characteristic
notes: Fuchs concludes that modulo two the sum of simplex counts equals the alternating sum, hence the Euler characteristic.
statement: For a finite triangulation \(K\), \(\sum_i f_i(K)\equiv\sum_i(-1)^if_i(K)=\chi(|K|)\pmod2\). The vertices of \(K^{\prime}\) correspond to nonempty simplices of \(K\), so its all-vertex zero-cycle has augmentation \(\chi(M)\bmod2\). For a closed \(n\)-manifold this is \(\langle w_n(TM),[M]\rangle\). Finiteness is essential to the elementary numerical sum.
reconstruction: The link between vertices of the subdivision and original simplices explains the otherwise compressed final line.
fate: \citet[\S1, discussion of \(C_0\), p.~512]{halperintoledo1972stiefel} identifies this zero-dimensional case with the Euler characteristic.

title: Frame bundle and vertical Maurer-Cartan identification
notes: For a real rank-\(n\) bundle \(E\to X\), a frame \(z\) is multiplied on the right by \(A\in GL(n,\mathbb R)\). Differentiating the orbit map identifies the vertical tangent space with the Lie algebra.
statement: For a smooth rank-\(n\) real vector bundle, its frame bundle \(P=\operatorname{Fr}(E)\) is a principal right \(GL(n,\mathbb R)\)-bundle. At \(z\in P_x\), the fundamental-vector map \(\alpha_z:\mathfrak{gl}_n\to V_zP\), \(\xi\mapsto\left.\frac{d}{dt}\right|_0 z\exp(t\xi)\), is an isomorphism; write \(\beta_z=\alpha_z^{-1}\). The action is free and transitive within each fiber, not on the whole frame bundle.
reconstruction: The right-action convention and distinction between a fiber and the total space are supplied explicitly.
fate: This principal-bundle framework underlies \citet[\S\S2--3]{garcia1972connections}; the source paper predates the seminar by four years.
present_status: As of 10 November 2026, the result is established in the stated scope.

title: Connection forms and equivariant horizontal complements
notes: A connection form \(\omega\) restricts to \(\beta_z\) vertically and satisfies \(R_A^*\omega=\operatorname{Ad}(A^{-1})\omega\). Its kernel is the horizontal space.
statement: For a smooth principal right \(G\)-bundle, a principal connection is a \(\mathfrak g\)-valued one-form \(\omega\) satisfying \(\omega(\xi^\#)=\xi\) and \(R_g^*\omega=\operatorname{Ad}_{g^{-1}}\omega\). Equivalently, \(TP=H\oplus VP\) with a smooth \(G\)-equivariant horizontal subbundle. For a frame bundle this corresponds to a linear connection on \(E\); the induced tangent-bundle connection is not automatically torsion-free.
reconstruction: The word affine in the notes is read as a connection on the tangent/frame bundle, without adding a torsion-free condition.
fate: Compare the connection-form and horizontal-distribution formulations used in \citet[\S3, proof of Theorem 3]{garcia1972connections}.
present_status: As of 10 November 2026, the result is established in the stated scope.

title: Affine fibers of pointwise connection data
notes: At \(z\), the space \(C_z\) of forms restricting to \(\beta_z\) is an affine plane parallel to the space \(\Theta_z\) of forms vanishing on vertical vectors.
statement: Define \(C_z=\{\eta\in\operatorname{Hom}(T_zP,\mathfrak g):\eta|_{V_zP}=\beta_z\}\) and \(\Theta_z=\operatorname{Hom}(T_zP/V_zP,\mathfrak g)\). Then \(C_z\) is an affine space modeled on \(\Theta_z\); subtraction of two elements is well defined, but there is no distinguished zero. The union \(C(P)\to P\) is a smooth affine bundle with its induced \(G\)-action.
reconstruction: The affine-torsor distinction is explicit: choosing one connection identifies fibers with vector spaces, but the identification is not canonical.
fate: The equivalent jet construction occurs in \citet[\S2, Theorems 1--2]{garcia1972connections}.
present_status: As of 10 November 2026, the result is established in the stated scope.

title: Connections as sections of an affine bundle over the base
notes: The quotient \(B(P)=C(P)/G\) is formed; connections correspond to its sections.
statement: For a smooth principal \(G\)-bundle \(P\to X\), let \(\mathcal C(P)=C(P)/G\). Smooth sections \(s:X\to\mathcal C(P)\) correspond bijectively to principal connections on \(P\): the equivariant lift chooses \(\omega_z\in C_z\) at every frame. Its affine model is \(T^*X\otimes\operatorname{ad}P\), where \(\operatorname{ad}P=P\times_G\mathfrak g\). For \(P=\operatorname{Fr}(E)\), this is \(T^*X\otimes\operatorname{End}(E)\).
reconstruction: The symbol \(\mathcal C(P)\) avoids confusing the quotient with the affine bundle over \(P\). The adjoint bundle, not a fixed global copy of \(\mathfrak g\), is necessary.
fate: \citet[Theorem 2, p.~236]{garcia1972connections} proves the section/connection correspondence.
present_status: As of 10 November 2026, the result is established in the stated scope.

title: The tautological universal connection and its correct base
notes: The notes call \(C(P)\) a principal bundle with a canonical connection, but state its base as \(P\).
statement: The principal bundle is \(C(P)\to\mathcal C(P)=C(P)/G\), naturally isomorphic to the pullback of \(P\to X\) along \(\mathcal C(P)\to X\). If \(p:C(P)\to P\), define \(\Omega_{(z,\eta)}(V)=\eta(dp(V))\). This reproduces fundamental vertical fields and is \(G\)-equivariant, hence is a principal connection. Pullback by the equivariant lift of a section \(s\) recovers precisely the connection represented by \(s\). The map to \(P\) has affine fibers and is not the asserted principal \(G\)-bundle.
reconstruction: The base-space correction and evaluation formula make the universal property precise; they are the intrinsic content of the displayed construction.
fate: This is the canonical connection of \citet[Theorem 3, pp.~238--240]{garcia1972connections}, expressed in pointwise connection data instead of jets.
present_status: As of 10 November 2026, the result is established in the stated scope.

title: Difference of connections as an endomorphism-valued one-form
notes: Gabrielov identifies the affine model, first writing a fixed Lie-algebra factor and then \(T^*X\otimes\operatorname{Hom}(E,E)\).
statement:
If \(
abla_1,
abla_2\) are linear connections on the same smooth vector bundle \(E\), their difference is \(C^\infty(X)\)-linear in the section and is a one-form in its vector argument: \(
abla_1-
abla_2\in\Omega^1(X;\operatorname{End}E)\). Conversely, adding any such one-form to a connection produces another connection. A fixed global \(\mathfrak{gl}_n\) coefficient space is valid only after a global trivialization of the adjoint bundle.
reconstruction: The final corrected bundle expression is retained; the crossed-out trivial coefficient bundle is not silently promoted to a global assertion.
fate: The affine structure is part of \citet[\S2, Theorem 2]{garcia1972connections}; its local Christoffel-symbol version is standard background.

title: Pointed-curve rings and their genus-zero and elliptic examples
notes: For a smooth projective curve and marked point, the ring consists of rational functions regular off that point. The examples are a genus-zero conic and \(y^2=x(x-1)(x-2)\), with pole orders two and three for \(x,y\). The latter are identified literally with \(\wp,\wp^{\prime}\).
statement: Let \(X\) be a smooth connected projective complex curve, \(P\in X\), and \(A=H^0(X\setminus\{P\},\mathcal O_X)\). For \((X,P)=(\mathbb P^1,\infty)\), \(A=\mathbb C[z]\). For the smooth projective completion of the displayed cubic and its point at infinity, \(A=\mathbb C[x,y]/(y^2-x(x-1)(x-2))\), with pole orders two and three. With \((\wp^{\prime})^2=4\wp^3-4\wp\), its correctly normalized uniformization is \(x=1+\wp\), \(y=\wp^{\prime}/2\). A genus-one curve has no nonconstant function with a unique simple pole, because that would define a degree-one map to \(\mathbb P^1\).
reconstruction: \oursComputed\ The normalization follows by substituting \(x=1+w\) into the cubic. The degree-one-map argument supplies the reason behind the notebook's torus remark; no new uniformization theorem is asserted.
fate: These are classical curve examples. The later exposition \citet[Ch.~II]{forster1981riemann} is cited for context; only its publisher record and author's contents were checked.
present_status: As of 10 November 2026, the result is established in the stated scope.

title: Recovering the pointed curve from its punctured function ring
notes: The ring is said to determine the curve and the point uniquely, followed by the question how to describe all such rings.
statement: The rings in question are precisely the finitely generated integrally closed complex domains of transcendence degree one whose smooth projective completion has exactly one point outside its affine spectrum. An isomorphism of such complex algebras identifies their function fields and affine curves, hence their unique smooth projective completions and the omitted points. The one-point condition is necessary: a general smooth affine curve may have several punctures.
reconstruction: The finite-generation, normality, transcendence-degree and one-point conditions are explicit reconstruction of the broad algebraic question. No intrinsic finite list of generators and relations is being claimed.
fate: This is the classical affine/projective correspondence for nonsingular curves; \citet[\S1]{drinfeld1977commutative} uses the fixed pointed-curve ring, without claiming the underlying correspondence as new.
present_status: As of 10 November 2026, the result is established in the stated scope.

title: Weierstrass gaps and the residue-class formula
notes: Krichever says that a general point has least pole order \(g+1\); a hyperelliptic branch point permits order two. If \(n\) is the least positive order and \(s+\mu_sn\) the least order in residue class \(s\), then \(\sum_{s=1}^{n-1}\mu_s=g\).
statement: For a smooth connected projective complex curve of genus \(g\), the pole-order semigroup \(H(P)\subset\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\) has exactly \(g\) positive gaps. At a non-Weierstrass point they are \(1,\ldots,g\). If \(n\) is its least positive nongap and \(s+\mu_sn\) is the least nongap congruent to \(s\pmod n\), then the gaps in that residue class are \(s,s+n,\ldots,s+(\mu_s-1)n\); consequently the asserted sum equals \(g\). On a smooth hyperelliptic curve of genus at least one, a branch point has a degree-two function with its only pole there. The hyperelliptic polynomial must have distinct roots.
reconstruction: The residue-class count explains the formula directly once the classical gap theorem is used. The genus and smoothness qualifications exclude degenerations hidden by the abbreviated equation.
fate: This is classical Riemann--Roch/Weierstrass-gap theory; see the later textbook context \citet[Ch.~II, \S\S16--18]{forster1981riemann}. The full textbook was not accessible.
present_status: As of 10 November 2026, the result is established in the stated scope.

title: Generators at an ordinary point and the missing generator
notes: The notes say there are \(g\) generators, then list orders \(g+1,g+2,\ldots,2g+1\).
statement: At a non-Weierstrass point of a genus-\(g\) smooth projective complex curve, choose functions with unique poles of orders \(g+1,\ldots,2g+1\), one for each order. These \(g+1\) functions generate \(A\). Indeed those integers generate the nongap semigroup: an order above \(2g+1\) can repeatedly be reduced by \(g+1\). A monomial with the same pole order as a given function can be scaled to cancel its leading term; induction reduces the remainder to a constant. This asserts a generating set, not an unconditional minimal number of algebra generators.
reconstruction: \ours\ The short leading-term induction is supplied to justify the emended count. It also includes genus zero, when the single generator has order one.
fate: The claim is an elementary consequence of the classical gap structure recalled in \citet[Ch.~II]{forster1981riemann}; the induction here is explicit reconstruction.

title: Elliptic homomorphisms and the pole/order rank revisited
notes: The differential algebra \(B[D]\), invertible leading coefficients, and the integer relation \(\operatorname{ord}\varphi(a)=n\deg_P a\) are recalled.
statement: For the pointed-curve ring \(A\), a commutative differential complex algebra \((B,\delta)\), and the Ore relation \(Db-bD=\delta(b)\), require \(\varphi:A\to B[D]\) to be unital, nontrivial in positive order, and to have unit leading coefficient for every nonzero image. Then its orders are a fixed positive integer multiple of pole orders, as in item 1975-380.5. The rank is that integer, not the degree of a chosen generator alone.

title: Leading coefficient and dependence on the local parameter
notes: For \(a=z^{-k}+\cdots\), the notes give \(\varphi(a)=b^kD^{nk}+\cdots\) and say that \(b\) is independent of \(k\) and of the chosen local parameter.
statement: With \(z\) fixed and the rank hypotheses above, a unique \(b\in B^*\) gives the normalized leading coefficients \(b^k\). The pole-order semigroup is cofinite, and multiplicativity makes the leading-coefficient homomorphism extend to its group completion \(\mathbb Z\). However, if \(\widetilde z=cz+O(z^2)\), \(c\ne0\), then \(\widetilde b=c^{-1}b\). Thus the scalar coefficient is not coordinate invariant. The corresponding tangent-direction datum, with the appropriate reciprocal coordinate factor, is intrinsic.

title: Gauge equivalence and local removal of a scalar connection term
notes: Two homomorphisms are equivalent under conjugation by \(b\in B^*\); the notes write \(D\sim D+b^{\prime}/b\), with an arbitrary function obtainable as a logarithmic derivative among germs.
statement: For a smooth nonvanishing complex function germ \(h\), \(h^{-1}Dh=D+h^{-1}h^{\prime}\), while \(hDh^{-1}=D-h^{-1}h^{\prime}\). The equivalence relation allows either orientation. Every smooth complex germ \(a\) is a logarithmic derivative of a unit germ, by solving \(h^{\prime}=ah\) with \(h(0)\ne0\). This local statement does not imply a periodic or global gauge exists.

title: Rank-one homomorphisms from a leading coefficient and a Jacobian point
notes: For germs of smooth functions on the line, rank-one homomorphisms up to equivalence correspond to their leading coefficient and a point of the Jacobian.
statement: Fix \((X,P,z)\) and let \(B\) be the algebra of smooth complex-valued germs at \(x=0\), with \(D=d/dx\). Rank-one Krichever homomorphisms \(A\to B[D]\), modulo unit scalar conjugation, correspond to pairs \((L_0,b)\), where \(b\in B^*\) and \(L_0\in\operatorname{Pic}^{g-1}(X)\) satisfies \(H^0(X,L_0)=H^1(X,L_0)=0\). The allowed line bundles form the complement of the theta divisor. Identifying this torsor with \(\operatorname{Jac}(X)=\operatorname{Pic}^0(X)\) requires a reference line bundle of degree \(g-1\). The construction is local in the coefficient parameter.

fate: \citet[Corollary 2]{drinfeld1977commutative} gives this precise correspondence, attributing it to Krichever.

title: Acyclic line bundles produce the pole filtration
notes: The filtration corresponds to a line bundle with vanishing zeroth and first cohomology, and \(M_i\) consists of sections with pole order at most \(i+1\) at \(P\).
statement: For a line bundle \(L\) on the smooth projective complex curve \(X\), assume \(H^0(X,L)=H^1(X,L)=0\). Then \(\deg L=g-1\). Put \(M=H^0(X\setminus\{P\},L)\), \(M_i=H^0(X,L((i+1)P))\) for \(i\ge-1\). The successive exact sequences at \(P\) and the vanishing of \(H^1(X,L)\) give \(\dim M_i=i+1\) and \(\dim M_i/M_{i-1}=1\) for \(i\ge0\). Over a coefficient algebra, use a locally free family with the corresponding cohomology and base-change conditions, not a tensor product of a fixed fiber assumed without justification.

title: Reconstructing the line bundle on two affine charts
notes: For nonconstant \(a_0\in A\), the cover is \((X\setminus P)\cup(X\setminus\operatorname{zeros}(a_0))\). On the second chart sections are \(m/a_0^k\), with \(m\in M_{k\deg(a_0)-1}\).

On \(U\cap V\) both localize to \(M[a_0^{-1}]\), so they glue. The filtration axioms give the line bundle extending across \(P\); the bound \(kd-1\) precisely cancels the allowed pole of order \(kd\).

title: Degree-zero divisor classes and line bundles
notes: S. Gelfand explains line bundles of degree zero as divisors \(\sum n_iQ_i\), \(\sum n_i=0\), modulo divisors of meromorphic functions.
statement: For a smooth connected projective complex curve, every line bundle admits a nonzero meromorphic section. Sending a divisor \(D\) to \(\mathcal O_X(D)\) identifies divisors modulo principal divisors with \(\operatorname{Pic}(X)\), and identifies degree-zero classes with \(\operatorname{Pic}^0(X)\). Changing the meromorphic section changes its divisor by a principal divisor, so its class is unchanged.

title: The period lattice and the analytic Jacobian
notes: The analytic definition uses \(g\) holomorphic differentials and \(2g\) period vectors, yielding \(\mathbb C^g/\Lambda\). On a smooth elliptic cubic, \(dx/y\) has no singularities even at branch points. Only some complex tori arise in this manner.
statement: For a compact connected Riemann surface of genus \(g\), \(V=H^0(X,\Omega_X^1)\) has complex dimension \(g\). Integration embeds \(H_1(X,\mathbb Z)\) as a lattice \(\Lambda\subset V^*\) of rank \(2g\); \(\operatorname{Jac}(X)=V^*/\Lambda\), canonically isomorphic to \(\operatorname{Pic}^0(X)\). On the nonsingular completion of \(y^2=x(x-a)(x-b)\), \(ab(a-b)\ne0\), \(dx/y\) extends holomorphically and without zeros. A branch coordinate such as \(y\), rather than \(x\), verifies regularity there. Jacobians carry a principal polarization; arbitrary complex tori need not be Jacobians.
reconstruction: The dual vector space, lattice rank, smoothness condition and polarization qualification are supplied. The note does not formulate a solution of the Schottky problem.
fate: The classical analytic construction is the subject of \citet[Ch.~II, \S\S20--21]{forster1981riemann}; verification here is bibliographic.

title: Jacobi inversion converts linear motion to moving divisors
notes: A straight line on the torus produces motion of \(g\) points on the curve.
statement: Fix a base point \(Q_0\). The Abel map \(\operatorname{Sym}^gX\to\operatorname{Jac}(X)\), \(Q_1+\cdots+Q_g\mapsto[Q_1+\cdots+Q_g-gQ_0]\), is generically one-to-one: a degree-\(g\) line bundle with \(h^0=1\) has a unique effective divisor. Thus a path \(Z(t)=Z_0+tU\) avoiding the exceptional/special-divisor locus locally determines an unordered moving divisor. Choosing and smoothly following individual ordered points further requires avoiding collisions. The inversion need not be globally single-valued in ordered points.
reconstruction: The generic-locus and collision restrictions make precise the drawing's motion statement. No differential equation for the individual points is asserted in the notes.
fate: This is the classical Jacobi inversion problem; compare \citet[Ch.~II, \S21]{forster1981riemann}.

title: Rank-one homomorphisms and filtered modules revisited
notes: The talk restates the rank-one order condition, scalar-gauge equivalence, exhaustive filtration and the two graded isomorphism conditions.
statement: Fix the smooth pointed projective curve and differential complex algebra \(B\). The rank-one Krichever homomorphism conditions and the filtered-module axioms of 1975-383.10 are equivalent, modulo a choice of generator of the free rank-one module \(M_0\). Explicitly, \(M=B[D]\), \(a\) acts by right multiplication with \(\varphi(a)\), and \(\nabla\) is left multiplication by \(D\). The nonzero images must have unit leading coefficient; zero has no such coefficient.

title: A nondifferential operator whose every higher power is differential
notes: Gelfand states that there is an operator whose second, third and all subsequent powers are differential operators, although the first is not.
statement: Interpret operator in the ring of formal pseudodifferential operators over \(\mathbb C(x)\). Set \(P=D^2-2/x^2\), \(R=D^3-3x^{-2}D+3x^{-3}\). They commute and satisfy \(R^2=P^3\). Hence \(Q=RP^{-1}\) obeys \(Q^2=P\), \(Q^3=R\); since every integer at least two is a nonnegative combination of two and three, all \(Q^m\), \(m\ge2\), are differential. But \(Q\) is not differential: its order and leading coefficient would force \(Q=D+a\), and comparison of the \(D\)-coefficient in \(Q^2=P\) gives \(a=0\), a contradiction. The same example works with smooth germs near any nonzero point.

fate: \citet[\S3, equations (2)--(3), and \S4]{mulase1990geometric} gives the commuting family and formal fractional-power framework.

title: The gap count recalled in residue-class form
notes: The least nongap \(n\), the integers \(\mu_i\), their sum \(g\), and the existence of exactly \(g\) missing pole orders are repeated.
statement: For a smooth connected projective complex curve of genus \(g\) and a point \(P\), the pole-order semigroup has \(g\) positive gaps. With \(n\) its least positive element and \(i+\mu_i n\) the least element in residue class \(i\), the count is \(g=\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}\mu_i\), as in 1975-383.3. This is a statement about functions having no poles away from \(P\), not about unrestricted meromorphic functions.

title: The reciprocal polar coefficient of the connection
notes: After choosing a local frame \(e\), the notes write \(\nabla e/e=1/(b_0z)+\cdots\), where \(b_0\) is the leading coefficient of the homomorphism.
statement: Fix the curve coordinate \(z\), and a local generator \(e\) of \(L\) near \(P\). If \(\nabla e=(b_0^{-1}z^{-1}+O(1))e\), \(b_0\in B^*\), then the principal-part datum is \(\beta=b_0^{-1}[z^{-1}]\). Multiplication by \(z^{-m}\) on the associated graded corresponds to \(b_0^m\nabla^m\), giving leading coefficient \(b_0^m\) for the operator attached to a normalized pole of order \(m\). title: Initial value and leading coefficient in the rank-one inverse correspondence
notes: The theorem is abbreviated to a point of the Jacobian in general position. The construction then uses a natural map \(B\to\mathbb C\), value at zero, to obtain \(L_0\).
statement: For \(B\) the algebra of smooth complex-valued germs at zero, evaluation \(B\to\mathbb C\) pulls the family back to its initial line bundle \(L_0\). Fixing a unit leading-coefficient germ \(b_0\), the gauge classes are parametrized by acyclic \(L_0\in\operatorname{Pic}^{g-1}(X)\). If \(b_0\) is not fixed, it is additional data and the Jacobian point alone is insufficient. For an arbitrary differential algebra \(B\), neither evaluation at zero nor this initial-value classification is automatic.

title: The Picard group and the tangent space of the Jacobian
notes: The tangent space is identified with \(H^1(X,\mathcal O_X)\), but the notes identify the whole Jacobian with \(H^1(X,\mathcal O_X^*)\).
statement: For a smooth compact connected complex curve, \(H^1(X,\mathcal O_X^*)=\operatorname{Pic}(X)\) includes all integer degrees. Its identity component is \(\operatorname{Pic}^0(X)=\operatorname{Jac}(X)\). The analytic exponential sequence gives \(\operatorname{Pic}^0(X)\cong H^1(X,\mathcal O_X)/\operatorname{im}H^1(X,\mathbb Z)\), with the conventional \(2\pi i\) factor according to the chosen exponential. Its tangent space at the identity, and by translation at any point, is \(H^1(X,\mathcal O_X)\). A fixed-degree Picard variety is a torsor for this group.
reconstruction: The missing degree-zero qualification is corrected; removing the star is interpreted as linearizing transition functions, not as a literal cohomology operation.
fate: The tangent-space identification is used in \citet[Corollary 2, proof]{drinfeld1977commutative}; the surrounding Picard theory is classical.

title: The principal-part boundary map gives the Jacobian velocity
notes: The class of \(1/z\) under the boundary map from \(\mathcal O_X(P)/\mathcal O_X\) is denoted \(\eta_P\), and \(\ell^{\prime}(x)=\eta_P/b_0(x)\). The final explanation identifies its line with the tangent to the Abel image of the curve.
statement: Let \(\delta_P:H^0(X,\mathcal O_X(P)/\mathcal O_X)\to H^1(X,\mathcal O_X)\) be the connecting homomorphism and put \(\eta_P=\delta_P([z^{-1}])\). For the smooth-germ rank-one data above, choose the Cech and divisor sign conventions consistently. The corresponding Picard path satisfies \(\ell^{\prime}(x)=b_0(x)^{-1}\eta_P\), hence locally \(\ell(x)=\ell(0)+\eta_P\int_0^x b_0(s)^{-1}\,ds\) in a lift to the universal cover. For \(g\ge1\), the line spanned by \(\eta_P\) is the tangent image of \(X\to\operatorname{Jac}(X)\), \(Q\mapsto[Q-P]\); a chosen tangent coordinate fixes its scale and convention fixes its sign. For genus zero the Jacobian and this vector vanish.
